item.title: Supreme Court upholds pause on Trump's anti-trans prison policy
item.description:
Criminal Justice
Supreme Court upholds pause on Trump's anti-trans prison policy
October 21, 202611:46 AM ET
Jaclyn Diaz
A view of the U.S. Supreme Court in Washington, DC, on October 14, 2026.
Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images/AFP
hide caption
toggle caption i
Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images/AFP
The Supreme Court ruled Wednesday that the Trump administration must continue providing gender-affirming care to transgender inmates in federal prisons.
The decision, in an emergency appeal, maintains a lower court's injunction on a federal Bureau of Prisons' policy that would terminate hormone therapy and other treatments for trans inmates.
The order offered no explanation behind the decision. It simply read, "The application for stay presented to The Chief Justice and by him referred to the Court is denied."
It also said Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito would side with the Trump administration and would grant the application for stay.
A federal district judge barred the BOP from implementing its policy this summer.
A second court, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, also rejected the administration's request to pause U.S. District Judge Royce Lamberth's order.

item.title: New human data hints at psychedelics' potential to combat inflammation
item.description:
Your Health
New human data hints at psychedelics' potential to combat inflammation
October 21, 202611:33 AM ET
By
Will Stone
Researchers are publishing some of the first data in humans that signals psilocybin holds potential for patients with neurodegenerative diseases.
Cannabis-Pic/Getty Images
hide caption
toggle caption i
Cannabis-Pic/Getty Images
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
Efforts to understand how classic psychedelics like psilocybin and LSD summon powerful changes in consciousness tend to focus on what's happening inside our head.
That's because these compounds bind tightly to serotonin receptors that densely populate certain structures of the brain, and a growing number of studies demonstrate they can exert long-lasting changes in mental health and well-being for people with a range of psychiatric conditions. Increasingly researchers have started to probe how these drugs elicit other physiological changes, given that many cells and tissues beyond the brain possess those same receptors, known as 5-HT2A.
Now, new research offers some of the first evidence in humans that psychedelics may also hold potential for treating diseases characterized by inflammation and immune dysregulation throughout the body.

item.title: Sentenced to death at 17, at 68, quilt artist receives solo museum exhibition
item.description:
Criminal Justice
Sentenced to death at 17, at 68, quilt artist receives solo museum exhibition
October 21, 202611:21 AM ET
By
Sea Stachura
Gary Tyler speaks about his work at the Grand Rapids Art Museum in Michigan. Behind Tyler are his quilts Big Toe, (2024) and Enduring, (2025). They feature two individuals who are incarcerated. He hopes his work draws attention to their plight and humanity.
Sea Stachura for NPR
hide caption
toggle caption i
Sea Stachura for NPR
Imagine living all of your adult life behind bars for a murder you didn't commit and being released at 58. You're also a fabric artist, and the Smithsonian has acquired one of your quilts. That's the story of Gary Tyler, and now, the artist has his first solo exhibit.
At the Grand Rapids Art Museum in Michigan, Gary Tyler points to a black-and-white quilt that's based on a photo.
"That's a picture that was taken by my brother back in [19]74," he says.
He was a 16-year-old with a flair for fashion, living in Louisiana. One school morning, he dressed in a body shirt with a sweater overtop. Then he added fingerless gloves and a bandana.
"This body shirt was the shirt and bandana that I had the day of the incident," he said.

item.title: Trump leans into unprecedented power ahead of midterm elections
item.description:
White House
Trump leans into unprecedented power ahead of midterm elections
October 21, 20268:09 AM ET
Franco Ordoñez
U.S. President Donald Trump boards Air Force One on October 19, 2026 in Joint Base Andrews, Maryland. President Trump is traveling to Kansas for a campaign rally.
Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images
hide caption
toggle caption i
Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images
President Trump boasted this weekend of his growing power in his second term – and all the things he's doing now that he wouldn't dare in his first term, such as changing the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America.
"I don't think I could have done this in my first term," he told supporters in Northern Kentucky, "This is a much more powerful term. I can do stuff that's unbelievable."
He joked about how big companies wouldn't take his call in the first term, but "now they kiss my ass."
Less than two weeks before the election, Trump continues to crash through barriers that he wouldn't dare cross in his first term – and pointing to that power to make his case to midterm voters.

item.title: 2025 policing trend: Fewer serious crimes, more minor arrests
item.description:
Criminal Justice
2025 policing trend: Fewer serious crimes, more minor arrests
October 21, 20265:00 AM ET
Jaclyn Diaz
Police arrest a man as the city of Philadelphia begins a clearing of a drug encampment in the Kensington section of Philadelphia on May 8, 2024.
Spencer Platt/Getty Images/Getty Images North America
hide caption
toggle caption i
Spencer Platt/Getty Images/Getty Images North America
Arrests for low-level crimes, including vagrancy and drug possession, rose in the U.S. from 2024 to 2025 even as rates of violent crime including homicide plummeted to historic national lows, according to a new analysis of federal data from the criminal justice and immigration reforms advocacy group FWD.us.
Zoë Towns, the executive director of FWD.us, spoke to NPR ahead of the report's release on Wednesday.
"This increase signals a really troubling return to some of the extreme law and order policies that defined the American criminal justice system during the 80s and the 90s," Towns said, referring to the era's tough-on-crime policies, including mandatory minimum prison sentences, that led to a massive rise in incarceration in the U.S. for decades.
